claim: Impaired respiratory motor output contributes to morbidity and mortality in many neurodegenerative diseases and neurologic injuries.
source: Impaired respiratory motor output contributes to morbidity and mortality in many neurodegenerative diseases and neurologic injuries.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established medical knowledge about respiratory complications in neurological conditions.

claim: Wild-type mice received bilateral intraspinal (C4) injections of AAV9-hSyn-HA-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry producing non-specific DREADD expression throughout the mid-cervical ventral horn.
source: Wild-type (C57Bl/6) and ChAT-Cre mice received bilateral intraspinal (C4) injections of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) encoding the hM3D(Gq) excitatory DREADD. In wild-type mice, this produced non-specific DREADD expression throughout the mid-cervical ventral horn.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure and resulting expression pattern in wild-type mice.

claim: ChAT-Cre mice received bilateral intraspinal (C4) injections using a Cre-dependent viral construct to drive neuronal DREADD expression in the C4 ventral horns, targeting phrenic motoneurons.
source: In ChAT-Cre mice, a Cre-dependent viral construct was used to drive neuronal DREADD expression in the C4 ventral horns, targeting phrenic motoneurons.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure for ChAT-Cre mice.

claim: The DREADD ligand JHU37160 (J60) caused a bilateral, sustained (>1 hr) increase in inspiratory EMG bursting in both wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice.
source: The DREADD ligand JHU37160 (J60) caused a bilateral, sustained (>1 hr) increase in inspiratory EMG bursting in both groups; the relative increase was greater in ChAT-Cre mice.
evidence: The abstract reports the experimental results from diaphragm EMG recordings.

claim: The relative increase in inspiratory EMG bursting after J60 administration was greater in ChAT-Cre mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: The DREADD ligand JHU37160 (J60) caused a bilateral, sustained (>1 hr) increase in inspiratory EMG bursting in both groups; the relative increase was greater in ChAT-Cre mice.
evidence: The abstract reports comparative results between the two mouse groups.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, intravenous J60 resulted in a sustained (>30 min) increase in tidal volume 3-4 months after intraspinal (C4) injection of AAV driving Cre-dependent hM3D(Gq) expression.
source: Three to four months after intraspinal (C4) injection of AAV driving Cre-dependent hM3D(Gq) expression, intravenous J60 resulted in a sustained (>30 min) increase in tidal volume.
evidence: The abstract reports results from plethysmography experiments in ChAT-Cre rats.

claim: Phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats under urethane anesthesia confirmed that J60 evoked a >200% increase in inspiratory output.
source: Subsequently, phrenic nerve recordings performed under urethane anesthesia confirmed that J60 evoked a >200% increase in inspiratory output.
evidence: The abstract reports results from phrenic nerve recordings.

claim: Neurologic injuries (e.g., traumatic spinal cord injury, stroke) and neurodegenerative conditions (e.g., amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Pompe disease) often result in decreased respiratory motor output, including impaired activation of phrenic motoneurons.
source: Neurologic injuries (e.g., traumatic spinal cord injury, stroke) and neurodegenerative conditions (e.g., amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Pompe disease) will often result in decreased respiratory motor output, including impaired activation of the phrenic motoneurons which innervate the diaphragm (Berlowitz et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2006; Perrin et al., 2004; Mehta, 2006; Burakgazi and Höke, 2010; Fuller et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Obstructive sleep apnea is associated with reduced pharyngeal motoneuron output during sleep.
source: Another prominent example is obstructive sleep apnea, in which pharyngeal motoneurons have reduced output during sleep (Jordan and White, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DREADDs are structurally derived from naturally occurring G-protein-coupled receptors and have been engineered to respond exclusively to exogenous ligands that are otherwise biologically inert.
source: Structurally derived from naturally occurring G-protein-coupled receptors, DREADDs have been engineered to respond exclusively to exogenous ligands that are otherwise biologically inert (Zhu and Roth, 2014; Alexander et al., 2009; Armbruster et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature describing DREADD technology.

claim: Prior studies have used DREADDs to stimulate upper airway muscle activation during breathing.
source: Prior studies have used DREADDs to stimulate upper airway muscle activation during breathing (Doyle et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Following expression of DREADDs in murine hypoglossal motoneurons, tongue EMG activity can be increased using DREADD ligands.
source: For example, following expression of DREADDs in murine hypoglossal motoneurons, tongue electromyogram (EMG) activity can be increased using DREADD ligands (Fleury Curado et al., 2017; Fleury Curado et al., 2018; Fleury Curado et al., 2021; Singer et al., 2022; Horton et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: DREADD-induced increase in tongue EMG activity is functionally beneficial as shown by increased patency of the upper airway.
source: This response is functionally beneficial as shown by increased patency of the upper airway (Fleury Curado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Phrenic motoneurons provide motor innervation of the diaphragm muscle and are located in the mid-cervical (C3–C5) spinal cord.
source: Phrenic motoneurons provide motor innervation of the diaphragm muscle and are located in the mid-cervical (C3–C5) spinal cord (Fuller et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-specific activation of cervical spinal networks can be highly effective at increasing diaphragm activation.
source: A compelling body of work, with studies in multiple species, demonstrates that non-specific activation of cervical spinal networks can be highly effective at increasing diaphragm activation (DiMarco and Kowalski, 2013; Jensen et al., 2019b; Alilain et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: One theory to explain effective diaphragm activation from non-specific cervical spinal stimulation is that a general increase in the excitability of cervical propriospinal networks leads to increased phrenic motoneuron activation.
source: One theory to explain this result is that a general increase in the excitability of cervical propriospinal networks leads to increased phrenic motoneuron activation (Satkunendrarajah et al., 2018; Jensen et al., 2019a; Lane, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is evidence that phrenic motoneurons can integrate multiple synaptic inputs in a manner that produces orderly recruitment.
source: There is also evidence that phrenic motoneurons can integrate multiple synaptic inputs in a manner that produces orderly recruitment (DiMarco and Kowalski, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In wild-type mice, the area under the curve (AUC) of the rectified and integrated diaphragm EMG was significantly increased after DREADD activation in both the left (p = 0.002) and right (p = 0.002) hemidiaphragm.
source: The area under the curve (AUC) of the rectified and integrated diaphragm EMG was significantly increased after DREADD activation (Figure 1d) in both the left (p = 0.002; Supplementary file 1) and right (p = 0.002; Supplementary file 1) hemidiaphragm.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from diaphragm EMG recordings in wild-type mice and references Figure 1d.

claim: In wild-type mice, the peak-to-peak amplitude of the rectified and integrated diaphragm EMG burst activity increased bilaterally following J60 administration (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.056; right hemidiaphragm: p = 0.01).
source: Additionally, the peak-to-peak amplitude of the rectified and integrated diaphragm EMG burst activity increased bilaterally following J60 administration (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.056; right hemidiaphragm: p = 0.01; Figure 1e; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from diaphragm EMG recordings in wild-type mice and references Figure 1e.

claim: In wild-type mice, both the left (p = 0.052) and right (p < 0.001) hemidiaphragm exhibited an increase in tonic activity following J60 administration.
source: Similar to the previous measures of EMG output both the left (p = 0.052; Supplementary file 1) and right (p < 0.001; Supplementary file 1) hemidiaphragm exhibited an increase in tonic activity following J60 administration.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from diaphragm EMG recordings in wild-type mice and references Figure 1f.

claim: In wild-type mice, there was no substantial change in respiratory rate after J60 administration (p = 0.863).
source: Notably, there was no substantial change in the respiratory rate of these spontaneous breathing mice after J60 administration (p = 0.863; Figure 1g; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from respiratory rate measurements in wild-type mice and references Figure 1g.

claim: In wild-type mice, five mice showed a bilateral increase in diaphragm output after J60 administration, four mice showed a response limited to the right hemidiaphragm, and two showed a response limited to the left hemidiaphragm.
source: Five mice showed a bilateral increase in diaphragm output after J60 administration (Figure 1), four mice showed a response that was limited to the right hemidiaphragm, and two showed a response that was limited to the left hemidiaphragm (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of responses across individual wild-type mice.

claim: All ChAT-Cre mice (n = 9/9) showed an increase in diaphragm EMG output in response to the J60 DREADD ligand in at least one hemidiaphragm.
source: All mice (n = 9/9) showed an increase in diaphragm EMG output in response to the J60 DREADD ligand in at least one hemidiaphragm (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the response rate in ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 2.

claim: In ChAT-Cre mice, both left (p = 0.011) and right (p < 0.001) diaphragm EMG AUC increased over time after J60 administration.
source: On average, both left (p = 0.011; Supplementary file 2) and right (p < 0.001; Supplementary file 2) diaphragm EMG AUC increased over time after J60 administration (Figure 2d).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from diaphragm EMG recordings in ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 2d.

claim: In ChAT-Cre mice, diaphragm EMG peak-to-peak amplitude had a bilateral increase following J60 delivery (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.013; right hemidiaphragm: p < 0.001).
source: Diaphragm EMG peak-to-peak amplitude had a similar, bilateral increase following J60 delivery (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.013; right hemidiaphragm: p < 0.001; Figure 2e; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from diaphragm EMG recordings in ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 2e.

claim: In ChAT-Cre mice, tonic activity showed an increase over time after J60 administration for both the left (p = 0.002) and right (p < 0.001) hemidiaphragm.
source: Lastly, tonic activity also showed an increase over time after J60 administration (Figure 2f) for both the left (p = 0.002; Supplementary file 2) and right (p < 0.001; Supplementary file 2) hemidiaphragm.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from diaphragm EMG recordings in ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 2f.

claim: In ChAT-Cre mice, respiratory rate decreased significantly over time after J60 administration (p < 0.001).
source: Respiratory rate decreased significantly over time after J60 administration (p < 0.001; Figure 2g; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from respiratory rate measurements in ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 2g.

claim: In ChAT-Cre mice, apart from two mice that showed a unilateral EMG response limited to the right hemidiaphragm, the remaining mice (n = 7/9) had bilateral increases in diaphragm EMG output following J60 administration.
source: Apart from two mice that showed a unilateral EMG response that was limited to the right hemidiaphragm the remaining ChAT-Cre mice (n = 7/9) had bilateral increases in diaphragm EMG output following J60 administration (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of responses across individual ChAT-Cre mice.

claim: Left hemidiaphragm responses to J60 were similar between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice across all outcome measures (AUC: p = 0.998; peak-to-peak amplitude: p = 0.771; tonic activity: p = 0.160).
source: Left hemidiaphragm responses to J60 were similar between the two groups across all outcome measures (AUC: p = 0.998; peak-to-peak amplitude: p = 0.771; tonic activity: p = 0.160; Figure 3a–c; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 3a-c.

claim: Right hemidiaphragm responses to J60 differed between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice across AUC (p = 0.0417), peak-to-peak amplitude (p = 0.00403), and tonic activity (p = 0.00207), with ChAT-Cre mice having larger magnitude responses.
source: However, right hemidiaphragm responses to J60 differed across AUC (Figure 3d), peak-to-peak amplitude (Figure 3e), and tonic activity (Figure 3f) with ChAT-Cre mice on average having larger magnitude responses compared to wild-type mice (AUC: p = 0.0417; peak-to-peak amplitude: p = 0.00403; tonic activity: p = 0.00207; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 3d-f.

claim: Respiratory rate was not different between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice (p = 0.382).
source: Respiratory rate was not different between the two groups (p = 0.382; Figure 3g; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons of respiratory rate between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice and references Figure 3g.

claim: Five of the eleven wild-type mice did not survive for the expected 90-minute recording duration.
source: However, five of the eleven total wild-type mice in this experiment did not survive for this duration.
evidence: The manuscript reports survival data for wild-type mice.

claim: All ChAT-Cre mice (n = 9/9) survived the total duration of the experimental protocol.
source: In contrast, all mice in the ChAT-Cre cohort (n = 9/9) survived the total duration of the experimental protocol.
evidence: The manuscript reports survival data for ChAT-Cre mice.

claim: A Chi-square evaluation of the survival proportions between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice was not statistically significant (Chi-squared = 3.2997, df = 1, p = 0.06929).
source: A Chi-square evaluation of the survival proportions was not statistically significant (Chi-squared = 3.2997, df = 1, p = 0.06929).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: In control experiments with animals not expressing hM3D(Gq), there was no discernable impact of J60 on diaphragm EMG burst amplitude (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.829; right hemidiaphragm: p = 0.496).
source: There was no discernable impact of J60 on the diaphragm EMG burst amplitude (mV) (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.829; right hemidiaphragm: p = 0.496; Figure 4a, b).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from control experiments and references Figure 4a-b.

claim: In control experiments, responses were not different between sham (saline) and J60 when normalized to baseline activity (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.832; right hemidiaphragm: p = 0.376).
source: Responses were also not different between sham (saline) and J60 when normalized to baseline activity (left hemidiaphragm: p = 0.832; right hemidiaphragm: p = 0.376; Figure 4c, d).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from control experiments and references Figure 4c-d.

claim: Four of four ChAT-Cre rats showed increased diaphragm EMG output after DREADD activation in anesthetized recordings.
source: ChAT-Cre rats (n = 4) underwent bilateral, intraspinal injections of AAV9-hSyn-DIO-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry into the ventral horns at C4 to introduce the hM3D(Gq) DREADD transgene into phrenic motoneurons. Four of four rats showed increased diaphragm EMG output after DREADD activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from diaphragm EMG recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, delivery of the J60 ligand resulted in an increase in inspiratory tidal volume compared to sham infusion (Normalized to Weight (ml/kg): Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.037).
source: Delivery of the J60 ligand resulted in an increase in inspiratory tidal volume compared to sham infusion (Normalized to Weight (ml/kg): Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.037; Figure 5a; Normalized to Baseline: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.091; Figure 5d; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from plethysmography experiments in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 5a and 5d.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, respiratory rate was unaffected by DREADD activation and was similar between sham and J60 conditions (Respiratory Rate: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.582).
source: Respiratory rate appeared to be unaffected by DREADD activation and was similar between sham and J60 conditions (Respiratory Rate: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.582; Figure 5b; Respiratory Rate Normalized to Baseline: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.774; Figure 5e; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from plethysmography experiments in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 5b and 5e.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, minute ventilation was slightly elevated in the J60 condition versus sham but did not reach statistical significance (Normalized to Body Weight: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.194).
source: Minute ventilation was slightly elevated in the J60 condition versus sham; however, this increase did not reach the threshold for statistical significance (Normalized to Body Weight: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.194; Figure 5c; Normalized to Baseline: Main effect of Treatment: p = 0.337; Figure 5f; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from plethysmography experiments in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 5c and 5f.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, there was no detectable relationship between time post-AAV injection and phrenic response to DREADD activation (Pearson correlation; left peak-to-peak response: p = 0.215; right peak-to-peak response: p = 0.318).
source: There was no detectable relationship between time post-AAV injection and phrenic response to DREADD activation (Pearson correlation; left peak-to-peak response: p = 0.215; right peak-to-peak response: p = 0.318).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the relationship between time post-injection and response magnitude.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of the J60 ligand caused a rapid, sustained, and bilateral increase in phrenic nerve efferent burst amplitude (left phrenic peak-to-peak amplitude: p < 0.001; Right phrenic peak-to-peak amplitude: p < 0.001).
source: Application of the J60 ligand caused a rapid, sustained, and bilateral increase in phrenic nerve efferent burst amplitude (left phrenic peak-to-peak amplitude (normalized to baseline): p < 0.001; Right phrenic peak-to-peak amplitude (normalized to baseline): p < 0.001; Figure 6b, c; Supplementary file 5), whereas saline injection had no impact.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6b-c.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, the increase in phrenic burst amplitude after J60 lasted up to 100 minutes post-administration.
source: The increase in phrenic burst amplitude lasted up to 100-min post-J60 administration, at which point the experiment was terminated.
evidence: The manuscript reports the duration of the phrenic nerve response.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of the J60 ligand resulted in an increase in phrenic tonic activity (left phrenic tonic activity: p < 0.001; right phrenic tonic activity: p < 0.001).
source: Application of the J60 ligand also resulted in an increase in phrenic tonic activity (left phrenic tonic activity (normalized to baseline): p < 0.001; right phrenic tonic activity (normalized to baseline): p < 0.001; Figure 6d, e; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6d-e.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of J60 did not affect heart rate (p = 0.587).
source: Application of J60 did not affect heart rate (p = 0.587; Figure 6h; Supplementary file 5) or respiratory rate (p = 0.282; Figure 6j; Supplementary file 5) but did result in a decrease in both systolic (p < 0.001; Figure 6f; Supplementary file 5) and diastolic blood pressure (p < 0.001; Figure 6g; Supplementary file 5) as well as MAP (p < 0.001; Figure 6i; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports cardiovascular measurements from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6h.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of J60 did not affect respiratory rate (p = 0.282).
source: Application of J60 did not affect heart rate (p = 0.587; Figure 6h; Supplementary file 5) or respiratory rate (p = 0.282; Figure 6j; Supplementary file 5) but did result in a decrease in both systolic (p < 0.001; Figure 6f; Supplementary file 5) and diastolic blood pressure (p < 0.001; Figure 6g; Supplementary file 5) as well as MAP (p < 0.001; Figure 6i; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports respiratory rate measurements from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6j.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of J60 resulted in a decrease in systolic blood pressure (p < 0.001).
source: Application of J60 did not affect heart rate (p = 0.587; Figure 6h; Supplementary file 5) or respiratory rate (p = 0.282; Figure 6j; Supplementary file 5) but did result in a decrease in both systolic (p < 0.001; Figure 6f; Supplementary file 5) and diastolic blood pressure (p < 0.001; Figure 6g; Supplementary file 5) as well as MAP (p < 0.001; Figure 6i; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports blood pressure measurements from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6f.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of J60 resulted in a decrease in diastolic blood pressure (p < 0.001).
source: Application of J60 did not affect heart rate (p = 0.587; Figure 6h; Supplementary file 5) or respiratory rate (p = 0.282; Figure 6j; Supplementary file 5) but did result in a decrease in both systolic (p < 0.001; Figure 6f; Supplementary file 5) and diastolic blood pressure (p < 0.001; Figure 6g; Supplementary file 5) as well as MAP (p < 0.001; Figure 6i; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports blood pressure measurements from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6g.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, application of J60 resulted in a decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) (p < 0.001).
source: Application of J60 did not affect heart rate (p = 0.587; Figure 6h; Supplementary file 5) or respiratory rate (p = 0.282; Figure 6j; Supplementary file 5) but did result in a decrease in both systolic (p < 0.001; Figure 6f; Supplementary file 5) and diastolic blood pressure (p < 0.001; Figure 6g; Supplementary file 5) as well as MAP (p < 0.001; Figure 6i; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports blood pressure measurements from phrenic nerve recordings in ChAT-Cre rats and references Figure 6i.

claim: All mice from both wild-type and ChAT-Cre cohorts showed evidence of mCherry expression in at least one segment of the mid-cervical spinal cord, with the exception of one ChAT-Cre mouse that was excluded from analysis.
source: All mice from both cohorts showed evidence of mCherry expression in at least one segment of the mid-cervical spinal cord (Figure 7) with the exception n = 1 ChAT-Cre mouse. This mouse was excluded from all analyses based on a priori exclusion criteria, which stipulated animals must show evidence of mCherry expression in the gray matter of at least one spinal segment from C3 to C6 to be included in the final analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports histological findings and references Figure 7.

claim: In wild-type mice, patterns of mCherry expression were relatively homogenous with the number of mice with positive expression increasing on the rostral-caudal axis.
source: Patterns of expression were relatively homogenous in wild-type animals. In this cohort, the number of mice with positive mCherry expression in the gray matter increased on the rostral–caudal axis.
evidence: The manuscript describes histological findings in wild-type mice.

claim: In ChAT-Cre mice, mCherry expression was more prevalent in the ventral horns and the right side of the cord.
source: In contrast, mCherry expression in the ChAT-Cre mice cohort was more prevalent in the ventral horns and the right side of the cord.
evidence: The manuscript describes histological findings in ChAT-Cre mice.

claim: In ChAT-Cre rats, mCherry expression was predominately in the ventral horns throughout the mid-cervical spinal cords with the highest levels of expression in spinal segments C4 and C5.
source: ChAT-Cre rats showed expression predominately in the ventral horns throughout the mid-cervical spinal cords with the highest levels of expression in spinal segments C4 and C5.
evidence: The manuscript describes histological findings in ChAT-Cre rats.

claim: Targeting mid-cervical spinal DREADD expression to the phrenic motoneuron pool enables ligand-induced, sustained increases in phrenic motor output and tidal volume.
source: We conclude that targeting mid-cervical spinal DREADD expression to the phrenic motoneuron pool enables ligand-induced, sustained increases in phrenic motor output and tidal volume.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental results.

claim: Further development of this technology may enable application to clinical conditions associated with impaired diaphragm activation and hypoventilation.
source: Further development of this technology may enable application to clinical conditions associated with impaired diaphragm activation and hypoventilation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: Phrenic motoneurons receive a rhythmic, monosynaptic, glutamatergic synaptic input from medullary neurons that produces phrenic motoneuron depolarization and subsequent diaphragm muscle contraction.
source: Phrenic motoneurons receive a rhythmic, monosynaptic, glutamatergic synaptic input from medullary neurons. Acting via NMDA and AMPA receptors, this produces phrenic motoneuron depolarization and subsequent diaphragm muscle contraction (Fuller et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Activating DREADDs on phrenic motoneurons should lower the threshold for activation via excitatory glutamatergic synaptic inputs, which would produce a greater output during the inspiratory phase.
source: Activating DREADDs on phrenic motoneurons should lower the threshold for activation via excitatory glutamatergic synaptic inputs, which would produce a greater output during the inspiratory phase.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on known DREADD function and phrenic motoneuron physiology.

claim: DREADD activation could directly lead to phrenic motoneuron action potentials even in the absence of synaptic input from the brainstem.
source: Alternatively, DREADD activation could directly lead to phrenic motoneuron action potentials even in the absence of synaptic input from the brainstem.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about how DREADDs might affect phrenic motoneurons.

claim: The tonic discharge observed after DREADD ligand delivery could be explained by direct DREADD-induced phrenic motoneuron action potentials occurring in the absence of synaptic input from the brainstem.
source: This latter possibility could explain the tonic discharge (i.e., EMG output across the entire respiratory cycle) that was noted to occur after delivery of the DREADD ligand.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed tonic discharge to a potential mechanism.

claim: Non-specific spinal cord DREADD expression in wild-type mice would likely produce an increase in the excitability and/or activation of phrenic motoneurons as well as propriospinal neurons in the immediate vicinity.
source: Non-specific spinal cord DREADD expression, as occurred in the wild-type mice (e.g., Figure 7a, ai), would likely produce an increase in the excitability and/or activation of phrenic motoneurons as well as propriospinal neurons in the immediate vicinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern observed in wild-type mice and references Figure 7a, ai.

claim: Neurophysiological and anatomical data confirm synaptic connections between mid-cervical interneurons and phrenic motoneurons.
source: Neurophysiological (Streeter et al., 2020), as well as anatomical data (Lane, 2011; Lane et al., 2008), confirm synaptic connections between mid-cervical interneurons and phrenic motoneurons, making it possible that DREADD activation of these interneurons impacted the diaphragm motor response in the wild-type mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: If DREADD-induced activation of the diaphragm leads to increased alveolar ventilation and metabolic rate is not impacted, then arterial CO2 values will decrease and the overall neural drive to breathe will also decrease.
source: For example, if DREADD-induced activation of the diaphragm leads to increased alveolar ventilation, and metabolic rate is not impacted, then arterial CO2 values will decrease and the overall neural drive to breathe will also decrease.
evidence: This is an inference based on established respiratory physiology.

claim: Vagal afferent feedback corresponding to increased lung volume has a powerful inhibitory impact on inspiration and therefore diaphragm activation.
source: Vagal afferent feedback corresponding to increased lung volume also has a powerful inhibitory impact on inspiration and therefore diaphragm activation.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge of respiratory control mechanisms.

claim: The sustained increase in diaphragm EMG and tidal volume observed following DREADD ligand application indicates that inhibitory feedback mechanisms were not sufficient to fully inhibit the increased phrenic motoneuron output.
source: However, the sustained increase in diaphragm EMG and tidal volume that we observed following application of the DREADD ligand indicates that these mechanisms, if activated, were not sufficient to fully inhibit the increased phrenic motoneuron output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: The relative increase in inspiratory motor output was considerably greater in the phrenic nerve recording experiments (~250% of baseline) compared to the diaphragm EMG response in spontaneously breathing animals (~100% of baseline).
source: The relative increase in inspiratory motor output was considerably greater in the phrenic nerve recording experiments (~250% of baseline) as compared to the diaphragm EMG response in spontaneously breathing animals (~100% of baseline).
evidence: This is a comparison of results from different experimental conditions.

claim: Vagal and/or blood gas-related inhibitory mechanisms may have somewhat constrained the response to the DREADD ligand in the spontaneously breathing animal.
source: This may indicate that vagal and/or blood gas-related inhibitory mechanisms, as mentioned above, somewhat constrained the response to the DREADD ligand in the spontaneously breathing animal.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference in response magnitude between experimental conditions.

claim: Variability in the laterality of mid-cervical mCherry expression and physiological response to the DREADD ligand in ChAT-Cre mice could have occurred due to subtle variations in animal positioning or needle tip placement.
source: However, we observed variability in the laterality (i.e., left vs. right side of the spinal cord) of mid-cervical mCherry expression as well as the physiological response to the DREADD ligand, particularly in the ChAT-Cre mice (e.g., Figure 2 and Figure 8). This could have occurred due to subtle variations of the positioning of the animal within the stereotaxic frame, and/or placement of the needle tip, leading to slight deviations for the desired coordinates between the left and right phrenic nuclei.
evidence: This is an inference to explain observed variability and references Figure 2 and Figure 8.

claim: The fluorophore (mCherry) expression observed in the experiments is clearly in the expected location of phrenic motoneurons.
source: However, the phrenic motor nucleus has been well described in the mouse (Qiu et al., 2010) and the rat (Rana et al., 2020; Rana et al., 2019), and the fluorophore (mCherry) expression observed in our experiments is very clearly in the expected location of phrenic motoneurons (Figure 7b–ci; Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and references multiple figures.

claim: The robust increase in phrenic motor output after the DREADD ligand is evidence of effective phrenic motoneuron targeting.
source: Further, the robust increase in phrenic motor output after the DREADD ligand, particularly in the ChAT-Cre rat experiment (Figure 6) is further evidence of effective phrenic motoneuron targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and references Figure 6.

claim: Cervical spinal cord directed chemogenetic receptors can be used to produce sustained increases in phrenic motor output, diaphragm activation, and inspiratory tidal volume.
source: Our data support the conclusion that cervical spinal cord directed chemogenetic receptors can be used to produce sustained increases in phrenic motor output, diaphragm activation, and inspiratory tidal volume.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: DREADDs should be directed exclusively to phrenic motoneurons versus non-specific expression in the immediate vicinity.
source: Collectively, the data indicate that DREADDs should be directed exclusively to phrenic motoneurons versus non-specific expression in the immediate vicinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative results between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice.

claim: Improvement of the AAV delivery methods will increase the selectivity of the approach for more precise targeting of phrenic motoneurons.
source: In this regard, improvement of the AAV delivery methods will increase the selectivity of the approach for more precise targeting of phrenic motoneurons.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed variability in expression patterns.

claim: Spinal cord chemogenetics may have application to clinical conditions associated with an inability to activate the diaphragm.
source: Concerning the 'translational value' of this work, spinal cord chemogenetics may have application to clinical conditions associated with an inability to activate the diaphragm.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications.

claim: After incomplete cervical spinal cord injury, focal expression of an excitatory DREADD in phrenic motoneurons could be used to increase the excitability of these cells, thereby improving the efficacy of spared bulbospinal synaptic inputs.
source: For example, incomplete cervical spinal cord injury is a condition in which the bulbospinal synaptic inputs to phrenic motoneurons are interrupted. After incomplete cervical spinal cord injury, focal expression of an excitatory DREADD in phrenic motoneurons could be used to increase the excitability of these cells, thereby improving the efficacy of spared bulbospinal synaptic inputs which convey 'inspiratory drive'.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential clinical application.

claim: The intraspinal AAV delivery used in this study was based on previous studies demonstrating successful gene delivery to phrenic motoneurons.
source: The intraspinal AAV delivery used here was based on previous studies demonstrating successful gene delivery to phrenic motoneurons (Alilain et al., 2008; Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mid-cervical spinal injections of an AAV5 vector encoding GAA in GAA null animals effectively restores spinal GAA enzyme activity.
source: For example, mid-cervical spinal injections of an AAV5 vector encoding the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) in animals with Pompe disease (GAA null) effectively restores spinal GAA enzyme activity (Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Spinal-delivered viral vectors have been used to successfully drive local expression of channelrhodopsin-2 to enable light activation of diaphragm output.
source: Spinal-delivered viral vectors have also been used to successfully drive local expression of channelrhodopsin-2 to enable light activation of diaphragm output (Alilain et al., 2008), and to drive expression of the astrocyte glutamate transporter GLT1 in the area of the phrenic motor nuclei (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intrapleural delivery effectively targets phrenic motoneurons in rodent models of cervical spinal cord injury and Pompe disease.
source: This technique (Mantilla et al., 2009) effectively targets phrenic motoneurons in rodent models of cervical spinal cord injury (Gransee et al., 2013; Martínez-Gálvez et al., 2016; Gransee et al., 2017) and Pompe disease (Keeler et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intramuscular diaphragm injection allows the vector to enter phrenic nerve terminals and reach phrenic motoneuron soma via retrograde movement.
source: Intramuscular diaphragm injection allows the vector to enter phrenic nerve terminals and reach phrenic motoneuron soma via retrograde movement (Thakre et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Direct diaphragm injection allows for relatively high target specificity, with the gene of interest expressed almost exclusively in phrenic motoneurons.
source: Direct diaphragm injection allows for a relatively high target specificity, with the gene of interest expressed almost exclusively in phrenic motoneurons (although expression can also occur in diaphragm myofibers, depending on the promoter sequence used).
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about viral vector delivery methods.

claim: In pilot experiments, intrapleural and intramuscular diaphragm injections using AAV9 vectors did not produce histological or physiological evidence of phrenic motoneuron transduction.
source: In pilot experiments, we tested intrapleural and intramuscular diaphragm injections using AAV9 vectors encoding GFP (AAV9-CAG-GFP) or DREADD (AAV9-hSyn-HA-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry and AAV9-hSyn-DIO-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry). We did not, however, observe histological or physiological evidence of phrenic motoneuron transduction with these AAV9 vectors.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from pilot experiments.

claim: Using different AAV serotypes or viruses with better retrograde movement could optimize the targeting of phrenic motoneurons.
source: We predict that using different AAV serotypes or viruses with better retrograde movement (e.g., 'AAV retro') could optimize the targeting of phrenic motoneurons (Tervo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the pilot experiment results and supported by a citation.

claim: DREADD technology is widely used for studying brain and spinal cord neuronal networks.
source: DREADD technology is widely used for studying brain and spinal cord neuronal networks (Smith et al., 2021; Roth, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Relatively few studies have examined if and how DREADDs can be used to activate or inhibit lower motoneurons.
source: Relatively few studies, however, have examined if and how DREADDs can be used to activate (or inhibit) lower motoneurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Two prior studies used pharmacologically selective actuator module to activate lumbar motoneurons in mouse models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Two of these studies used pharmacologically selective actuator module, a type of ionotropic chemogenetic receptor, to activate lumbar (Ouali Alami et al., 2020; Saxena et al., 2013) motoneurons, in mouse models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Excitatory DREADDs were applied to spinal motoneurons to improve axon regeneration following peripheral nerve injury.
source: In the remaining studies, excitatory DREADDs were applied to spinal motoneurons to improve axon regeneration following peripheral nerve injury (Jaiswal et al., 2018; Jaiswal and English, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies show that once hM3D(Gq) is expressed in XII motoneurons, DREADD ligands will rapidly produce an increase in the EMG activation of tongue muscles.
source: Collectively, these studies show that once hM3D(Gq) is expressed in XII motoneurons, DREADD ligands will rapidly produce an increase in the EMG activation of tongue muscles (Fleury Curado et al., 2021; Singer et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The increase in tongue muscle output after DREADD activation tends to manifest as an increase in the inspiratory-related activation and tonic discharge across the respiratory cycle.
source: This increase in tongue muscle output tends to manifest as an increase in the inspiratory-related activation and tonic discharge across the respiratory cycle.
evidence: This statement draws on prior studies of hypoglossal DREADD activation.

claim: XII motoneuron DREADD expression has been suggested as a possible treatment for obstructive sleep apnea.
source: Since increased tongue muscle activation can promote patency of the upper airway, XII motoneuron DREADD expression has been suggested as a possible treatment for obstructive sleep apnea (Fleury Curado et al., 2017; Fleury Curado et al., 2021; Horton et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The primary innovation of the present study is the first application of DREADD technology to phrenic motoneurons.
source: For the present study, the primary innovation is the first application of DREADD technology to phrenic motoneurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work.
